content.text: I'll start by checking the trace and metric schemas, then look at where latency first moves.

input.query: SELECT service_name, count(*) n, approx_quantile(duration/1e6, 0.95) p95_ms, avg(duration/1e6) avg_ms, sum(CASE WHEN attr_status_code='Error' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) errs FROM abnormal_traces GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY p95_ms DESC
SELECT service_name, count(*) n, approx_quantile(duration/1e6, 0.95) p95_ms, avg(duration/1e6) avg_ms FROM normal_traces GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY p95_ms DESC

content.text: The overall latency shifts are spread across several services. Next I'll break down the key services by pod and by span name to see where the time is added.

input.query: SELECT 'abn' p, service_name, attr_k8s_pod_name pod, attr_span_kind kind, count(*) n, approx_quantile(duration/1e6,0.5) p50, approx_quantile(duration/1e6,0.95) p95 FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name IN ('ts-basic-service','ts-route-service','ts-travel-service','ts-seat-service','ts-preserve-service','ts-route-plan-service','ts-travel-plan-service') GROUP BY ALL UNION ALL SELECT 'norm', service_name, attr_k8s_pod_name, attr_span_kind, count(*), approx_quantile(duration/1e6,0.5), approx_quantile(duration/1e6,0.95) FROM normal_traces WHERE service_name IN ('ts-basic-service','ts-route-service','ts-travel-service','ts-seat-service','ts-preserve-service','ts-route-plan-service','ts-travel-plan-service') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 2,3,1

content.text: Route-service and basic-service tails grew while their median time stayed flat. Next I'll compare metric means across the two periods for every service to look for resource pressure.

input.query: WITH a AS (SELECT 'abn' p, service_name, metric, avg(value) m, count(*) n FROM abnormal_metrics GROUP BY ALL), n AS (SELECT 'norm' p, service_name, metric, avg(value) m, count(*) n FROM normal_metrics GROUP BY ALL) SELECT coalesce(a.service_name,n.service_name) svc, coalesce(a.metric,n.metric) met, round(n.m,3) norm_mean, round(a.m,3) abn_mean, a.n abn_n, n.n norm_n FROM a FULL OUTER JOIN n ON a.service_name=n.service_name AND a.metric=n.metric WHERE abs(coalesce(a.m,0)-coalesce(n.m,0)) > 0.2*greatest(abs(coalesce(n.m,0)),0.0001) AND coalesce(a.service_name,n.service_name) LIKE 'ts-%' ORDER BY svc, met

content.text: Preserve-service's container CPU rose about eightfold, and ts-seat-service's queueSize dropped. Next I'll look at the CPU timeline per minute for the main suspects.

input.query: SELECT service_name, metric, date_trunc('minute', time) t, round(avg(value),3) v FROM abnormal_metrics WHERE service_name IN ('ts-preserve-service','ts-route-service','ts-basic-service','ts-route-plan-service') AND metric IN ('container.cpu.usage','jvm.system.cpu.utilization','k8s.pod.cpu.usage') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY service_name, metric, t

content.text: The metrics look sparse, so I'll check onset directly: per-minute p95 of server spans for the key services across the abnormal window.

input.query: SELECT service_name, date_trunc('minute', time) t, count(*) n, round(approx_quantile(duration/1e6,0.5),1) p50, round(approx_quantile(duration/1e6,0.95),1) p95 FROM abnormal_traces WHERE attr_span_kind='Server' AND service_name IN ('ts-preserve-service','ts-route-service','ts-basic-service','ts-route-plan-service','ts-travel-plan-service','ts-seat-service','ts-travel-service') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY service_name, t

content.text: Route-service's own time climbs from 01:24 and preserve-service's tail starts around 01:22. Next I'll check restarts, uptime and log errors for the affected services.

input.query: SELECT 'metric' src, metric svc_or_level, service_name, count(*) n, round(min(value),2) mn, round(max(value),2) mx FROM abnormal_metrics_sum WHERE metric IN ('k8s.container.restarts','k8s.pod.uptime') GROUP BY ALL UNION ALL SELECT 'log', level, service_name, count(*), 0, 0 FROM abnormal_logs WHERE level <> 'INFO' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 1,3

content.text: No restarts or uptime resets. The error logs that matter are in preserve-service and ui-dashboard, so I'll read those messages.

content.text: The sampled traces are dominated by loadgen retries, so I need a service-wide view. I'll check the CPU time series for every service to find the one that saturates first.

input.query: SELECT service_name, date_trunc('minute', time) t, round(avg(CASE WHEN metric='container.cpu.usage' THEN value END),3) cpu, round(avg(CASE WHEN metric='jvm.system.cpu.utilization' THEN value END),3) jvmcpu, round(avg(CASE WHEN metric='k8s.pod.cpu_limit_utilization' THEN value END),3) lim FROM abnormal_metrics WHERE metric IN ('container.cpu.usage','jvm.system.cpu.utilization','k8s.pod.cpu_limit_utilization') AND service_name LIKE 'ts-%' GROUP BY ALL HAVING cpu > 0.2 ORDER BY t, service_name

content.text: The CPU bursts are scattered and don't single out one service. I'll look at each service's outgoing calls by span pair to see which callee accounts for the added time at route-plan, travel-plan and preserve.

input.query: WITH ab AS (SELECT span_id, trace_id, service_name svc, span_name, attr_span_kind kind, duration, parent_span_id FROM abnormal_traces), ac AS (SELECT span_id, service_name svc, attr_span_kind kind, duration, parent_span_id FROM normal_traces) SELECT 'abn' p, c.service_name caller, c.span_name, a.svc callee_svc, count(*) n, round(approx_quantile(c.duration/1e6,0.5),1) p50, round(approx_quantile(c.duration/1e6,0.95),1) p95 FROM abnormal_traces c JOIN ab a ON a.parent_span_id=c.span_id WHERE c.service_name IN ('ts-route-plan-service','ts-travel-plan-service','ts-preserve-service','ts-basic-service','ts-travel-service') AND c.attr_span_kind='Client' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY caller, n DESC

content.text: Several shared callees (route, basic, seat) show tail growth, which points to a shared dependency rather than one service. I'll check whether the affected pods share a node and what node utilization looks like.

input.query: SELECT 'abn' p, attr_k8s_node_name node, service_name, round(avg(CASE WHEN metric='k8s.pod.cpu.node.utilization' THEN value END),4) node_util, round(avg(CASE WHEN metric='k8s.pod.cpu.usage' THEN value END),3) pod_cpu, count(DISTINCT attr_k8s_pod_name) pods FROM abnormal_metrics WHERE service_name IN ('ts-route-service','ts-basic-service','ts-seat-service','ts-travel-service','ts-preserve-service','ts-route-plan-service','ts-travel-plan-service','ts-travel2-service','ts-mysql','mysql','rabbitmq','ts-ui-dashboard') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY node, service_name

content.text: Node utilization is negligible everywhere, so this is not node saturation. Route and basic degrade progressively in the last two minutes, which suggests something building up inside a process. I'll look at JVM heap and GC metrics for route, basic and seat.

input.query: SELECT service_name, metric, date_trunc('minute', time) t, round(avg(value),3) v FROM abnormal_metrics WHERE service_name IN ('ts-route-service','ts-basic-service') AND (metric LIKE 'jvm.gc%' OR metric LIKE 'jvm.memory%' OR metric LIKE 'jvm.thread%' OR metric LIKE '%gc%' OR metric LIKE '%heap%') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY service_name, metric, t

SELECT 'sum' src, metric, count(*) n, count(DISTINCT service_name) svcs FROM abnormal_metrics_sum GROUP BY metric UNION ALL SELECT 'hist', metric, count(*), count(DISTINCT service_name) FROM abnormal_metrics_histogram GROUP BY metric ORDER BY 1,2

content.text: Pool metrics are flat in both periods, so the database pool is not the cause. Basic-service's own internal time has the largest tail growth, so I'll break down its internal spans by name.

input.query: SELECT 'abn' p, span_name, attr_span_kind kind, count(*) n, round(approx_quantile(duration/1e6,0.5),1) p50, round(approx_quantile(duration/1e6,0.95),1) p95 FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-basic-service' GROUP BY ALL UNION ALL SELECT 'norm', span_name, attr_span_kind, count(*), round(approx_quantile(duration/1e6,0.5),1), round(approx_quantile(duration/1e6,0.95),1) FROM normal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-basic-service' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 2,1

content.text: Basic's own method time and its outgoing client calls both grew in the tail. To separate wire delay from callee slowness, I'll compare each caller's client span with the callee's matching server span, for both periods.

content.text: The largest client-minus-server gaps cluster on calls into route-service, but drops are zero and the gaps are modest, so the wire is probably not the main story. Basic's `queryForTravel(s)` self-time grew about 5x at p95 while p50 stayed flat, which looks like a method-level slowdown. I'll check whether slow basic internal spans have slow children or not.

input.query: WITH slow AS (SELECT span_id, trace_id, duration FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-basic-service' AND attr_span_kind='Internal' AND span_name LIKE 'BasicController%' AND duration > 150e6 LIMIT 6) SELECT s.span_id parent, round(s.duration/1e6,1) parent_ms, c.service_name, c.span_name, c.attr_span_kind, round(c.duration/1e6,1) ms, c.attr_k8s_pod_name pod FROM slow s JOIN abnormal_traces c ON c.trace_id=s.trace_id AND c.parent_span_id=s.span_id ORDER BY parent, c.time

content.text: In the slow basic spans, one client call accounts for almost all of the time (for example 285 ms out of 314 ms). I'll identify which callee those slow calls go to and what the callee's server span reports.

input.query: SELECT c.span_name, c.attr_k8s_pod_name cpod, c.attr_k8s_pod_name, count(*) n_slow, round(avg(c.duration/1e6),1) cli_ms, round(avg(s.duration/1e6),1) srv_ms, any_value(s.service_name) callee, any_value(s.attr_k8s_pod_name) callee_pod FROM abnormal_traces c LEFT JOIN abnormal_traces s ON s.parent_span_id=c.span_id AND s.attr_span_kind='Server' WHERE c.service_name='ts-basic-service' AND c.attr_span_kind='Client' AND c.duration > 100e6 GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n_slow DESC

content.text: The slow calls from basic go to ts-station-service and ts-train-service, and their server spans are slow too (94 ms and 440 ms). I'll check those two callees' server spans and their children.

content.text: Station's slow server spans spend their time inside the controller method itself, not in child spans. Before deciding it's a service-internal stall, I'll check the network side: pod network errors and hubble TCP-flag counts.

input.query: WITH a AS (SELECT service_name, metric, attr_k8s_pod_name pod, avg(value) v FROM abnormal_metrics_sum WHERE metric IN ('k8s.pod.network.errors','hubble_tcp_flags_total','hubble_drop_total') GROUP BY ALL), n AS (SELECT service_name, metric, attr_k8s_pod_name pod, avg(value) v FROM normal_metrics_sum WHERE metric IN ('k8s.pod.network.errors','hubble_tcp_flags_total','hubble_drop_total') GROUP BY ALL) SELECT coalesce(a.metric,n.metric) met, coalesce(a.service_name,n.service_name) svc, round(sum(n.v),1) norm_sum, round(sum(a.v),1) abn_sum, count(*) pods FROM a FULL JOIN n USING (service_name, metric, pod) GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY met, abn_sum DESC LIMIT 60

content.text: There are no network errors or drops anywhere, so the network is not the cause. Preserve-service is the one service with a unique CPU burst and a class-loading shift, so I'll pull its full metric timeline.

input.query: SELECT metric, date_trunc('second', time) t, round(avg(value),3) v FROM abnormal_metrics WHERE service_name='ts-preserve-service' AND metric NOT LIKE 'hubble%' GROUP BY ALL HAVING metric IN ('container.cpu.usage','k8s.pod.memory.page_faults','jvm.system.cpu.utilization','k8s.pod.cpu.usage') ORDER BY metric, t

Other investigators, each starting fresh with the same tools, checked your draft answer: the kind of each fault, and how each fault's effect travelled. Their findings:

### `ts-preserve-service`: you said `container_cpu_saturated`. They conclude `process_cpu_saturated` (confidence: low).
Scope: Claim rejected: ts-preserve-service did not suffer container_cpu_saturated. Its container CPU did burst to about 3.6 cores from 01:21:39 to 01:22:44, but the pod peaked at only 0.64 of its CPU limit and the JVM showed no matching CPU use. Its worst latency (01:24-01:25) came after the burst ended, and its own Internal span tracks its Server span, so the time is spent in downstream calls. Those callees (ts-basic, ts-food, ts-route, ts-seat) also slow in that window without a CPU signature. The source of the latency is not identified here; the one unexplained item is the short non-JVM CPU burst.
Ruled out:
- `container_cpu_saturated`: Pod CPU-limit utilization peaks at 0.644 (about 3.6 cores against an implied limit near 5.6), so the cgroup is not pinned. JVM process CPU (jvm.cpu.recent_utilization) is about 0 during the burst. Preserve's server p95 is worst at 01:24-01:25 (5156 ms and 6751 ms) when container CPU is back to 0.04-0.14 cores, so latency does not track the CPU burst.

Scope: Affects ts-basic-service's outgoing calls to ts-route-service, ts-station-service, ts-train-service and ts-price-service, and so the Server spans of its callers (ts-travel2, ts-travel, ts-preserve). - `pod_unavailable`: Same evidence as pod_failure: no restarts, and basic keeps emitting metrics and spans through the abnormal window, with inbound calls to it reduced in proportion to traffic rather than stopping.

kind_checks.scope: Claim rejected: ts-preserve-service did not suffer container_cpu_saturated. Its container CPU did burst to about 3.6 cores from 01:21:39 to 01:22:44, but the pod peaked at only 0.64 of its CPU limit and the JVM showed no matching CPU use. Its worst latency (01:24-01:25) came after the burst ended, and its own Internal span tracks its Server span, so the time is spent in downstream calls. Those callees (ts-basic, ts-food, ts-route, ts-seat) also slow in that window without a CPU signature. The source of the latency is not identified here; the one unexplained item is the short non-JVM CPU burst.

ruled_out.why: Pod CPU-limit utilization peaks at 0.644 (about 3.6 cores against an implied limit near 5.6), so the cgroup is not pinned. JVM process CPU (jvm.cpu.recent_utilization) is about 0 during the burst. Preserve's server p95 is worst at 01:24-01:25 (5156 ms and 6751 ms) when container CPU is back to 0.04-0.14 cores, so latency does not track the CPU burst.

Survey Hubble data shows zero drops on every preserve-related pod pair, and the slowdown is spread across several downstream callees rather than confined to preserve's links. Not separately queried; based on the survey table.

content.text:
**Verdict: the evidence does not support `container_cpu_saturated` for `ts-preserve-service`. I'd put low-to-moderate confidence on rejecting it, and I couldn't identify the kind that fits instead.**

**What the lead's evidence shows:** Container CPU does jump from about 0.06 to 3.6 cores between 01:21:39 and 01:22:44, then returns to baseline. Preserve's server p95 does rise, from about 535 ms normal to 869–5156 ms in the burst minutes. Both numbers are correct. The lead's reading of them is what fails.

**Evidence against container saturation:**

1. **The pod never reached its CPU limit.** Peak `k8s.pod.cpu_limit_utilization` is 0.644, and the 3.6-core peak implies a limit of roughly 5.6 cores. A cgroup-saturated container would sit at or near 1.0 of its limit.
2. **The JVM process is not the one burning CPU.** `jvm.cpu.recent_utilization` is about 0 at 01:22:45 and 0.001 at 01:23:45. The metric is sparse, so this is weak, but it does not show the JVM driving the burst.
3. **Latency does not follow the CPU burst.** The CPU burst ends at about 01:22:45. Preserve's worst latency comes later, at 01:24 (Server p95 5156 ms) and 01:25 (p95 6751 ms), while container CPU is back at 0.04–0.14 cores. A process-wide CPU saturation would slow the handler while the burst lasts, not minutes after it ends.
4. **Preserve's own time is not the slow part.** `PreserveController.preserve` (Internal) tracks its Server span almost exactly, so the time is spent inside the handler's calls. Its Client spans to downstream services carry the growth.
5. **The downstream services slow in the same window, with no CPU pattern.** Server p95 for ts-basic, ts-food, ts-route and ts-seat all rises at 01:24–01:25, while their request rates fall. ts-seat's mean container CPU is unchanged from normal (0.30 vs 0.31). A shared downstream effect, not preserve's own CPU, is the more likely source of the latency.
6. **No drops in the network data.** Hubble `drops` are 0 on every connection listed in the survey, so there is no sign of packet loss on preserve's links.

**Caveats:**
- The 3.6-core burst is a real anomaly and is not explained by these data. It might be a short non-JVM process, a sidecar, or something I didn't check.
- The `k8s.pod.cpu_limit_utilization` figure is the only limit signal here. I did not find a direct limit metric, so the "not at limit" reading depends on it.
- I did not separate `network_delay` from `http_slow` or `application_method_slow` for the downstream calls. That is outside this check, and I'd need a per-peer Client-vs-Server gap analysis to decide it.
- Logs for preserve were not checked; my query used a column name that does not exist in this table.

Basic's own controller processing (own time per span), its container CPU, and its restart count are not affected. The extra time is an irregular long tail on every connection out of basic, while the median of those calls stays normal.

ruled_out.why: The claimed kind is rejected. Own time (span duration minus child spans) of BasicController.queryForTravel moves only from p95 7.7 ms to 11.0 ms and p50 stays about 5 ms; queryForTravels own p95 goes 7.3 to 8.7 ms. The 40 to 245 ms rise in controller spans is almost entirely time waiting on child Client calls.

Client span p50 to each callee is flat (route 8.6 to 8.7 ms, station 5.2 to 5.6, train 6.0 to 6.0, price 6.5 to 6.5). Delay would shift every call by a similar amount; here only the tail grows, with a scatter from 25 ms to about 2.4 s.

The slowdown appears on every callee and on both GET and POST client spans, not on particular HTTP routes. Other routes between the same services are equally affected, so the fault is not confined to particular HTTP requests.

Basic's container.cpu.usage averages 0.224 normal and 0.225 abnormal, and k8s.pod.cpu_limit_utilization falls from 0.045 to 0.039. Only brief spikes (max 0.94) appear. Container CPU is not pinned, and basic's own method time did not grow.
k8s.container.restarts is 0 in both periods, and basic's metric rows are present in both periods at the same sample count (48 per metric), so basic was not stopped or restarted.
Same evidence as pod_failure: no restarts, and basic keeps emitting metrics and spans through the abnormal window, with inbound calls to it reduced in proportion to traffic rather than stopping.

The lead investigator's evidence for it:

Code has also surveyed this case's telemetry; the survey follows. Use it as a starting point and check it: it may miss what matters.

## Survey of this case, computed by code

A starting point, not the answer: it ranks nothing out. Check what it shows, and look beyond it.
Pairs are normal → abnormal. Rates are per minute; latencies are p95 in milliseconds; `own` is a span's time minus its children's; `metric` is the service's largest shift in normal-period standard deviations; `onset` is seconds into the abnormal window of the first minute outside the service's normal range.

content.text: I'll start by checking whether the slowdown is inside basic's process or on the wire, comparing Server, Internal and Client spans on basic, normal against abnormal.

input.query: SELECT 'normal' period, service_name, attr_span_kind, span_name, count(*) n, round(approx_quantile(duration/1e6,0.5),1) p50, round(approx_quantile(duration/1e6,0.95),1) p95 FROM normal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-basic-service' GROUP BY ALL HAVING count(*)>20 UNION ALL SELECT 'abnormal', service_name, attr_span_kind, span_name, count(*) n, round(approx_quantile(duration/1e6,0.5),1) p50, round(approx_quantile(duration/1e6,0.95),1) p95 FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-basic-service' GROUP BY ALL HAVING count(*)>20 ORDER BY 3,4,1

WITH c AS (SELECT trace_id, span_id, service_name peer, span_name, duration FROM abnormal_traces WHERE attr_span_kind='Client' AND service_name IN ('ts-travel2-service','ts-travel-service','ts-preserve-service') AND span_name LIKE '%basic%'), s AS (SELECT trace_id, parent_span_id, duration FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-basic-service' AND attr_span_kind='Server') SELECT count(*) n, round(approx_quantile(c.duration/1e6,0.5),1) client_p50, round(approx_quantile(s.duration/1e6,0.5),1) server_p50, round(approx_quantile(c.duration/1e6,0.95),1) client_p95, round(approx_quantile(s.duration/1e6,0.95),1) server_p95 FROM c JOIN s ON s.parent_span_id=c.span_id AND s.trace_id=c.trace_id

content.text: The join returned nothing because the Client span names are bare verbs. I'll join on span IDs alone, then compare basic's outgoing calls with the callee's Server spans to find where the extra time sits.

input.query: WITH cl AS (SELECT 'normal' per, trace_id, span_id, service_name caller, duration d FROM normal_traces WHERE attr_span_kind='Client' AND service_name='ts-basic-service' UNION ALL SELECT 'abnormal', trace_id, span_id, service_name, duration FROM abnormal_traces WHERE attr_span_kind='Client' AND service_name='ts-basic-service'), sv AS (SELECT 'normal' per, trace_id, parent_span_id, service_name callee, duration d FROM normal_traces WHERE attr_span_kind='Server' UNION ALL SELECT 'abnormal', trace_id, parent_span_id, service_name, duration FROM abnormal_traces WHERE attr_span_kind='Server') SELECT cl.per, sv.callee, count(*) n, round(approx_quantile(cl.d/1e6,0.5),1) client_p50, round(approx_quantile(sv.d/1e6,0.5),1) server_p50, round(approx_quantile(cl.d/1e6,0.95),1) client_p95, round(approx_quantile(sv.d/1e6,0.95),1) server_p95 FROM cl JOIN sv ON sv.parent_span_id=cl.span_id AND sv.trace_id=cl.trace_id AND sv.per=cl.per GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 2,1

WITH p AS (SELECT 'normal' per, trace_id, span_id, span_name, duration FROM normal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-basic-service' AND attr_span_kind='Internal' AND span_name LIKE 'BasicController%' UNION ALL SELECT 'abnormal', trace_id, span_id, span_name, duration FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-basic-service' AND attr_span_kind='Internal' AND span_name LIKE 'BasicController%'), ch AS (SELECT 'normal' per, trace_id, parent_span_id, sum(duration) cd FROM normal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-basic-service' GROUP BY ALL UNION ALL SELECT 'abnormal', trace_id, parent_span_id, sum(duration) FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-basic-service' GROUP BY ALL) SELECT p.per, p.span_name, count(*) n, round(approx_quantile(p.duration/1e6,0.5),1) p50, round(approx_quantile(p.duration/1e6,0.95),1) p95, round(approx_quantile((p.duration-coalesce(ch.cd,0))/1e6,0.5),1) own_p50, round(approx_quantile((p.duration-coalesce(ch.cd,0))/1e6,0.95),1) own_p95 FROM p LEFT JOIN ch ON ch.trace_id=p.trace_id AND ch.parent_span_id=p.span_id AND ch.per=p.per GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 2,1

content.text:
**Verdict: `application_method_slow` is not supported.** The telemetry points to the time being lost in basic's outgoing calls, not in its own methods. I'd lean toward a network-level tail fault on basic's connections, which is a low-to-moderate confidence call (see below).

**What disproves the claim**

- **Basic's own time barely moves.** Own time is span duration minus child spans. For `BasicController.queryForTravel`, own p95 goes 7.7 → 11.0 ms and own p50 stays at about 5 ms. For `queryForTravels`, own p95 goes 7.3 → 8.7 ms. The 40 → 245 ms rise in the controller spans is almost entirely time spent waiting on child calls.
- **The slow children are basic's outgoing calls, and their median is unchanged.** Basic's Client spans to its callees show p50 flat and p95 raised:

| Callee | Client p50 (normal → abnormal) | Client p95 (normal → abnormal) | Callee Server p95 (normal → abnormal) |
|---|---|---|---|
| route | 8.6 → 8.7 | 11.2 → 64.6 | 8.4 → 36.8 |
| station | 5.2 → 5.6 | 7.3 → 34.3 | 4.2 → 10.7 |
| train | 6.0 → 6.0 | 7.8 → 25.6 | 4.5 → 5.2 |
| price | 6.5 → 6.5 | 9.2 → 24.6 | 5.8 → 8.8 |

- **The slowdown is not specific to one route or method.** It affects every callee, and the same pattern appears in the Client spans of GET and POST.
- **The tail is irregular.** Basic's GET client spans in the abnormal period have about 1,373 under 25 ms, then a long scatter from 25 ms out to about 2.4 s, with a few isolated points at 1.1 s and 2.35 to 2.4 s. A steady extra amount would look different.
- **No resource saturation in basic.** Container CPU usage averages 0.224 normal and 0.225 abnormal, with spikes up to 0.94. Restarts are 0 in both periods. Pod CPU limit utilization falls slightly.

**What this suggests**

Irregular, long-tailed extra time on every connection out of basic, with normal median and no change in basic's own processing, fits a transport-level fault. It matches `network_loss` (or `network_partition`, which is in the same equivalence class). It does not match `network_delay`, which would shift every call by a similar amount, or `http_slow`, which would be route-specific.

**Caveats**

- The callee Server spans also grew in the tail, most clearly for route (p95 8.4 → 36.8). Route may also be affected, which a pure link fault would not explain. The survey's own-time figures for route stayed flat, so this is unresolved.
- Hubble drop counters are 0 in the abnormal period, and per-connection flow counts only roughly doubled. I did not check the `hubble_*` metrics directly for basic's connections, so this is not a clean read on loss.
- I did not compare basic's logs against the normal period. The abnormal log count is 6,367 lines and I did not check their content.
- Loss and partition cannot be separated from these tables, and the evaluator scores them as one answer.

**Confidence:** high that `application_method_slow` is wrong for basic. Moderate-to-low that the evidence supports network loss on basic's outgoing links specifically, rather than a fault further along route/station/train/price.

The extra time is an irregular long tail on every connection out of basic, while the median of those calls stays normal.","ruled_out":[{"kind":"application_method_slow","why":"The claimed kind is rejected. Callee Server p95 also rises for route (8.4 to 36.8) and station (4.2 to 10.7), less so for train and price. The rise in total controller time comes from child Client calls, which is what rules out application_method_slow."},{"sql":"SELECT 'normal' per, metric, round(avg(value),3) avg_v, round(max(value),3) max_v, count(*) n FROM normal_metrics WHERE attr_k8s_pod_name LIKE 'ts-basic%' AND (metric LIKE 'container.cpu%' OR metric LIKE 'k8s.pod.cpu%' OR metric LIKE 'jvm.gc%' OR metric LIKE 'jvm.memory.used' OR metric LIKE 'k8s.container.restarts%' OR metric LIKE 'k8s.pod.uptime%') GROUP BY ALL UNION ALL SELECT 'abnormal', metric, round(avg(value),3), round(max(value),3), count(*) FROM abnormal_metrics WHERE attr_k8s_pod_name LIKE 'ts-basic%' AND (metric LIKE 'container.cpu%' OR metric LIKE 'k8s.pod.cpu%' OR metric LIKE 'jvm.gc%' OR metric LIKE 'jvm.memory.used' OR metric LIKE 'k8s.container.restarts%' OR metric LIKE 'k8s.pod.uptime%') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 2,1","claim":"Basic's container.cpu.usage averages 0.224 (normal) vs 0.225 (abnormal), max 0.42 vs 0.94. k8s.container.restarts is 0 in both periods (24 samples each). k8s.pod.cpu_limit_utilization averages 0.045 vs 0.039. evidence.claim: Preserve's calls to ts-basic-service changed: normal 145 calls at 40.9 ms p95 and 0 errors; abnormal 98 calls at 179.3 ms p95 and 0 errors. Calls fell by about a third while latency rose about 4x, so basic's slowdown reached preserve through this outgoing link.

spread_checks.reasoning: The fault's effect reached the entry tier by one direct route: ts-preserve-service slowed down, and ts-ui-dashboard's calls to it got much slower and fewer. Preserve's outgoing calls to ts-basic-service also got slower, so basic carried the effect back into preserve. I rejected the travel, route-plan and travel-plan cluster (the draft's basic-to-travel and route-plan-to-ui links) because its slowdown began about 0-21 s into the incident, well before preserve's onset at about 149 s, and basic is slow for all of its callers, not just preserve. I also left out preserve's other callees (travel, food, security, seat, assurance, user, contacts, order) because their slowdowns come mostly from their own downstream calls rather than from preserve's fault.

WITH t AS (SELECT 'normal' per, * FROM normal_traces UNION ALL SELECT 'abnormal', * FROM abnormal_traces),
c AS (SELECT per, span_id, service_name callee, duration FROM t WHERE attr_span_kind='SPAN_KIND_SERVER'),
p AS (SELECT per, span_id, service_name caller, duration pd FROM t WHERE attr_span_kind='SPAN_KIND_CLIENT')
SELECT p.caller, c.callee,
 p.per,
 COUNT(*) n,
 ROUND(quantile_cont(c.duration,0.95)/1e6,1) callee_p95_ms,
 ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN c.attr_status_code='STATUS_CODE_ERROR' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END),3) err

WITH t AS (SELECT 'normal' per, * FROM normal_traces UNION ALL SELECT 'abnormal', * FROM abnormal_traces),
c AS (SELECT per, parent_span_id, service_name callee, duration, attr_status_code sc FROM t WHERE attr_span_kind='Server'),
p AS (SELECT per, span_id, service_name caller FROM t WHERE attr_span_kind='Client')
SELECT p.caller, c.callee, c.per, COUNT(*) n,
 ROUND(quantile_cont(c.duration,0.95)/1e6,1) callee_p95_ms,
 ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN c.sc='Error' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END),3) err
FROM c JOIN p ON c.per=p.per AND c.parent_span_id=p.span_id
WHERE p.caller IN ('ts-preserve-service','ts-basic-service','ts-travel-service','ts-travel2-service','ts-route-plan-service','ts-travel-plan-service','ts-ui-dashboard')
  AND c.callee IN ('ts-basic-service','ts-travel-service','ts-travel2-service','ts-route-plan-service','ts-travel-plan-service','ts-preserve-service','ts-seat-service','ts-station-service','ts-route-service','ts-food-service')
GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY 1,2,3

SELECT metric_name, attr_k8s_pod_name, attr_k8s_node_name, COUNT(*) n, ROUND(AVG(value),2) avgv FROM abnormal_metrics WHERE metric_name IN ('k8s.pod.cpu.node.utilization') AND (attr_k8s_pod_name LIKE 'ts-preserve%' OR attr_k8s_pod_name LIKE 'ts-basic%' OR attr_k8s_pod_name LIKE 'ts-travel%' OR attr_k8s_pod_name LIKE 'ts-route%' OR attr_k8s_pod_name LIKE 'ts-food%' OR attr_k8s_pod_name LIKE 'ts-seat%' OR attr_k8s_pod_name LIKE 'ts-ui%') GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY 3,2

content.text:
**Answer: two propagation edges carry the fault from `ts-preserve-service` toward the user-facing tier.**

1. **ts-preserve-service → ts-ui-dashboard.** This is the direct link. Entry-tier `ts-ui-dashboard` calls to preserve went from 524 ms to 1,324 ms p95, and calls fell from 36.3 to 24.8 per minute. Preserve's own time rose from 10 to 36 ms, starting about 149 s into the incident, which matches the fault.

2. **ts-basic-service → ts-preserve-service.** This is the outgoing-request link. Preserve's calls to basic went from 40.9 ms to 179 ms p95 (about 4x), with calls falling from 36.3 to 24.5 per minute. Basic's own time also rose (5.9 to 13.5 ms). This is the largest slowdown among preserve's callees, so I'm keeping the draft's edge.

**Edges from the draft that I did not confirm for this fault:**

- **ts-basic-service → ts-travel-service**, **ts-basic-service → ts-travel2-service**, **ts-travel-service → ts-route-plan-service**, **ts-travel2-service → ts-route-plan-service**, **ts-route-plan-service → ts-travel-plan-service**, **ts-travel-plan-service → ts-ui-dashboard.** The link changes are real (for example, travel calling basic went from 42 to 195 ms p95, and travel-plan calling route-plan from 696 to 1,162 ms). But this cluster's onset is about 0–21 s, well before preserve's 149 s, and basic is slow for every caller, not just preserve. The data points to a separate slowdown around basic, not to preserve's fault. I'd leave these out of this fault's propagation unless a check shows preserve's fault reaching basic.

**Preserve's other callees, which I rejected:**

- Travel, food, security, seat, assurance, user, contacts and order all show slower calls from preserve. Most of that is inherited from their own downstream slowdowns (travel's from basic, for example), and their own processing time barely moved. None shows a clear, independent slowdown that starts at preserve's onset, so I didn't add edges for them.

**Limits:** I used 7 of the roughly 10 planned queries. I did not check per-node CPU placement, which would show whether basic shares a node with preserve. That check could change the answer for the travel cluster and for the other callees.

spread_checks.reasoning: The delay from ts-basic-service spreads to its callers along three routes that all end at ts-ui-dashboard: basic → travel/travel2 → route-plan → travel-plan → ui, basic → preserve → ui, and basic → travel → food → ui. Travel and travel2 also reach ui directly, and travel also feeds preserve and food, so the effect arrives by several routes. Every edge shows latency growth with no errors and fewer calls, consistent with a slowdown. Basic's outgoing calls to ts-price-service, ts-route-service, ts-station-service and ts-train-service were left out: their call volume fell in step with basic's own throughput and their own latencies barely moved, so they did not carry the effect back to basic's callers, although route-service's p95 as seen from basic rose from 8 to 36 ms and is the one ambiguous signal.

input.query:
WITH p AS (
 SELECT 'normal' per, service_name, span_id, parent_span_id, duration, attr_status_code FROM normal_traces
 UNION ALL SELECT 'abn', service_name, span_id, parent_span_id, duration, attr_status_code FROM abnormal_traces),
pairs AS (
 SELECT c.per, par.service_name AS caller, c.service_name AS callee, c.duration, c.attr_status_code
 FROM p c JOIN p par ON c.parent_span_id = par.span_id AND c.per = par.per
 WHERE c.service_name <> par.service_name)
SELECT caller, callee,
 SUM(CASE WHEN per='normal' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) n_norm,
 SUM(CASE WHEN per='abn' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) n_abn,
 ROUND(quantile_cont(CASE WHEN per='normal' THEN duration END, 0.95)/1e6,1) p95_norm,
 ROUND(quantile_cont(CASE WHEN per='abn' THEN duration END, 0.95)/1e6,1) p95_abn,
 SUM(CASE WHEN per='abn' AND attr_status_code='ERROR' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) err_abn
FROM pairs
WHERE callee IN ('ts-basic-service','ts-travel-service','ts-travel2-service','ts-preserve-service','ts-food-service','ts-route-plan-service','ts-travel-plan-service','ts-ui-dashboard')
  AND caller IN ('ts-ui-dashboard','ts-travel-service','ts-travel2-service','ts-preserve-service','ts-food-service','ts-route-plan-service','ts-travel-plan-service','ts-basic-service')
GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 1,2

WITH p AS (
 SELECT 'normal' per, service_name, span_id, parent_span_id, duration, attr_span_kind FROM normal_traces
 UNION ALL SELECT 'abn', service_name, span_id, parent_span_id, duration, attr_span_kind FROM abnormal_traces),
pairs AS (
 SELECT c.per, par.service_name AS caller, c.service_name AS callee, par.duration pdur, c.duration cdur
 FROM p c JOIN p par ON c.parent_span_id = par.span_id AND c.per = par.per
 WHERE c.service_name <> par.service_name AND par.service_name='ts-basic-service')
SELECT callee, per, COUNT(*) n, ROUND(quantile_cont(pdur,0.95)/1e6,1) parent_basic_p95, ROUND(quantile_cont(cdur,0.95)/1e6,1) child_p95, ROUND(quantile_cont(pdur-cdur,0.5)/1e6,1) gap_median
FROM pairs GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 1,2

content.text:
The fault at `ts-basic-service` reached the user-facing tier through 14 links. The draft had 8 of them. I confirmed each link with a caller-callee span comparison (normal vs. incident) and found no errors on any of them, so the effect is latency, not failures.

**Edges (called service → caller, direction of failure travel)**

From the draft, all confirmed:
1. ts-basic-service → ts-travel-service (caller p95 42→195 ms; calls 557→357 in the sample)
2. ts-basic-service → ts-travel2-service (48→260 ms)
3. ts-basic-service → ts-preserve-service (41→179 ms)
4. ts-travel-service → ts-route-plan-service (192→353 ms)
5. ts-travel2-service → ts-route-plan-service (256→308 ms)
6. ts-route-plan-service → ts-travel-plan-service (696→1,163 ms)
7. ts-travel-plan-service → ts-ui-dashboard (871→1,651 ms)
8. ts-preserve-service → ts-ui-dashboard (524→1,324 ms)

Missing from the draft, found by the span check:
9. ts-travel-service → ts-ui-dashboard (369→418 ms)
10. ts-travel2-service → ts-ui-dashboard (255→415 ms)
11. ts-travel-service → ts-preserve-service (331→536 ms; preserve calls travel)
12. ts-travel-service → ts-food-service (14→72 ms; food calls travel)
13. ts-food-service → ts-ui-dashboard (45→145 ms)
14. ts-food-service → ts-preserve-service (15→53 ms)

Edges 12–14 form a second route: basic → travel → food → preserve/ui-dashboard. Edges 9–11 are direct calls from travel/travel2/preserve to the users' entry point, skipping route-plan and travel-plan.

**Links left out**

- ts-price-service, ts-route-service, ts-station-service and ts-train-service → ts-basic-service. These are calls basic makes to its dependencies. Their call volume fell by about 37%, the same as basic's own throughput, and their own service latencies barely moved. The fault is slowness inside basic's method, not in its outgoing requests, so I did not count these as carrying the effect. Route-service's p95 as seen from basic rose 8→36 ms, which is the one ambiguous signal here; I left it out, but it is the first link to revisit if the lead wants a stricter reading.
